title: Trump’s New “Coalie” Mascot and Myth of “Clean, Beautiful Coal” have a Long History in Advertising
author: Annie Persons
content:
![](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732945/original/file-20260429-57-cuwv6t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&rect=0%2C0%2C768%2C512&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)

_Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posted this cartoon of himself with ‘Coalie,’
a lump of coal.[Interior Secretary Doug
Burgam/X](https://x.com/SecretaryBurgum/status/2014382110828536183?lang=en)_

If you follow the Trump administration’s social media posts, you might spot
its new mascot: a cartoon lump of coal with big eyes and babylike features.
“Coalie” [sparked a backlash](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/feb/03/trump-administration-coalie-mascot-fossil-fuels) almost as
soon as Interior Secretary [Doug Burgum debuted
it](https://x.com/SecretaryBurgum/status/2014382110828536183?lang=en) for the
Office of Surface Mining and Reclamation Enforcement in early 2026.

Coalie’s design [draws on a type of Japanese anime called
Kawaii](https://grist.org/culture/trump-coal-mascot-coalie-cute-burgum/), a
word [meaning “cute” or “adorable.”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/kawaii-
culture) It’s the latest in the White House’s efforts to pass off coal as
harmless, despite the well-established [environmental and human health
harms](https://www.catf.us/resource/cradle-to-grave-the-environmental-impacts-
from-coal/) of mining and burning the fossil fuel.

As a scholar of American literature and culture, I [write about media
portrayals of coal](https://online.ucpress.edu/ncl/article-
abstract/80/1/38/212053/Hawthorne-and-the-Ongoing-Age-of-Coal), beginning in
the 19th century with its rise to become the leading fuel in the United
States. Coal use grew until the early 2000s, when other sources became cheaper
and its health and environmental damage became unacceptable to more of the
public.

While “Coalie” might be new, the logic behind it is not. For centuries, coal’s
promoters have worked hard to show coal as harmless – as well as [“clean” and
“beautiful,”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VcTeS0IH9O0) to use President
Donald Trump’s words.

**" An Agreeable Heat"**

Humans living with the effects of burning coal have disliked it for as long as
they have burned it.

In 1578, Queen Elizabeth complained that she was “greatly grieved and annoyed
with [its] taste and smoke” in the air. In 1661, [John Evelyne’s treatise
Fumifugium](https://web.english.upenn.edu/%7Ecavitch/pdf-
library/Evelyn_Fumifugium.pdf) outlined negative health effects of breathing
coal smoke.

[![The front page of a pamphlet published in 1661 with the title and test,
including 'the inconveniencie of the aer and smoak of
London.'](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732948/original/file-20260429-57-k21gir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=237&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732948/original/file-20260429-57-k21gir.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)In
his 1661 treatise Fumifugium, John Evelyne described health risks from
breathing coal smoke. [University of California San Diego
Libraries/Wikimedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumifugium#/media/File:John_Evelyn's_Fumifugium,_Title_Page.jpg)

English settlers were drawn to North America in part because of the
continent’s [abundant supply of
timber](https://martinhopp.com/media/articles/history-of-the-lumber-industry-
in-north-america), a substitute for coal that deforestation had made
prohibitively expensive in England.

But by the 19th century, [the price of timber had risen in America as
well](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w33974/w33974.pdf).
When, in the 1820s, [news spread of Pennsylvania’s rich veins of anthracite
coal](https://archive.org/details/homefireshowamer0000adam/page/n5/mode/2up),
urban consumers were eager for a cheaper source of fuel.

In addition to its lower price, anthracite coal grew desirable because of its
high carbon, low-sulfur content, which produced less visible smoke when it was
burned. An [enthusiastic 1815
letter](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732950/original/file-20260429-57-mpli66.png)
to the editor of the American Daily Advertiser captured [increasingly common
attitudes toward
anthracite](https://archive.org/details/homefireshowamer0000adam/page/n5/mode/2up)
as “affor[ding] a very regular and agreeable heat.”

**‘A healthful home’**

The spread of anthracite also shored up tolerance for smokier but cheaper
bituminous coal.

To help people, housekeeping manuals aimed at the fossil fuel’s [mostly female
users](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/398013285_Making_Coal_Sharp_Gendered_Consumers_and_Users_of_Mineral_Fuel_in_the_19th_Century_United_States)
tried to invent workarounds for its smoke. In 1869, Harriet Beecher Stowe,
best known as the author of “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” and her sister Catharine
Beecher wrote one of many 19th-century articles to [acknowledge the “evils” of
coal
smoke](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732953/original/file-20260429-57-ahi8m7.png),
while outlining “modes of making a healthful home,” in the housekeeping manual
[American Woman’s Home](https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000708605).

Consumers provided temporary solutions for maintaining indoor air quality
while burning coal by sending in suggestions that were published in
housekeeping manuals, magazines and newspapers.

[![An add reading 'Why
not?'](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732954/original/file-20260429-57-iobirx.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732954/original/file-20260429-57-iobirx.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)An
1892 advertisement in the Rocky Mountain News promoted a brand of coal stoves
as ‘the best, handsomest and most economical.’ [Nineteenth Century
Newspapers](https://gale.com/product-catalog/225178).

At the same time, as the century progressed, coal and coal-stove companies
began to suggest that burning coal was healthy, that it could improve indoor
air as well as domestic aesthetics. One 1892 newspaper advertisement claimed
that stoves were “necessary to heat, cheer, and beautify the home and preserve
its health.”

**To keep the children clean and bright …**

In the 20th century, marketers churned out more colorful claims about the
benefits of coal: One [magazine advertisement](https://madison-
historical.siue.edu/archive/items/show/2116) showed a mother and child
pointing at the crackling stove aflame with the company’s coal, saying it
“cannot be excelled in purity, cleanliness, and free-burning qualities.”

[![An ad with a woman and child with a coal
stove.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732955/original/file-20260429-57-ege1ge.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732955/original/file-20260429-57-ege1ge.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)An
ad for a coal stove described its ‘purity’ and ‘cleanliness.’  
[Madison Historical](https://madison-
historical.siue.edu/archive/items/show/2116), [CC BY-NC-
SA](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/)

Similarly, the Lackawanna Railroad Company came up with the classy, often
rhyming, character of Phoebe Snow. In one ad, she points to the [importance of
comfort](https://posterhouse.org/blog/who-was-phoebe-snow/), suggesting that
not only could anthracite fuel faster travel, but it could also make your
travel – and your life – more comfortable.

[![A postcard ad for Lackawanna Railroad featuring Phoebe Snow, wearing white,
talks about its use of anthracite
coal.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733175/original/file-20260430-72-pwkyg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733175/original/file-20260430-72-pwkyg9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)A
Phoebe Snow postcard ad from 1912 talked about avoiding ‘smoke and cinders’
with trains run on anthracite coal. [Railroad Museum of Pennsylvania/Wikimedia
Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/76/Phoebe_Snow_Postcard_1912_%28higher_quality%29.jpg)

Coal marketing often used children to suggest safety and reach parents.
Another iteration of the Phoebe Snow series promised that anthracite-powered
railway travel could keep children “[clean and
bright](https://posterhouse.org/blog/who-was-phoebe-snow/).”

[![Two women sit in a train car talking with well-behaved, very clean
children.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733558/original/file-20260501-57-chwzx3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733558/original/file-20260501-57-chwzx3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)One
of the Phoebe Snow ads, in 1910, advertised Lackawanna Railway’s coal-powered
trains using children and whiteness to suggest purity.  
[Photo Courtesy of Poster House/Poster House Permanent
Collection](https://posterhouse.org/blog/who-was-phoebe-snow/)

A 1930s advertisement went so far as to position a piece of anthracite [coal
next to a child in a
bathtub](https://www.etsy.com/listing/1630417092/1930s-advertising-blotter-
for-famous), a visual proximity implying that coal was as good as soap.

In fact, soap made of “[coal tar](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/causes-
prevention/risk/substances/coal-tar)” – a liquid byproduct of producing coke,
a fuel made from bituminous coal used in industrial blast furnaces – did ([and
does](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/psoriasis/treatment/medications/coal-
tar)) exist. The British company Wright’s, also popular in the U.S., generated
a slew of [advertisements praising its
soap](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732959/original/file-20260429-57-aphewz.jpg)
as having antiseptic properties for children.

[![A smiling woman stands over a sleeping child in an ad for coal tar
soap.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732959/original/file-20260429-57-aphewz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732959/original/file-20260429-57-aphewz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)Wright’s
Coal Tar Soap used a sleeping child dressed in white and sleeping on white
sheets to advertise its ‘nursery soap,’ which it claimed protected children
from infection, in 1922. [Wikimedia
Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright%27s_Coal_Tar_Soap#/media/File:Wright's_Coal_Tar_Soap,_1922.jpg)

Each of these advertisements tried to capitalize on a mother’s desire for
healthy children. And they pushed back against the image of the tyrannical
“[King
Coal](https://archive.org/details/kingcoalnov00sincrich/page/n9/mode/2up)”
that had come about amid [strikes by miners
protesting](https://energyhistory.yale.edu/coal-mining-and-labor-conflict/)
dangerous, degraded working and living conditions as well as the rise of
[black lung](https://www.lung.org/lung-health-diseases/lung-disease-
lookup/black-lung) disease.

**‘Clean coal’**

By the mid-20th century, [petroleum took coal’s place as America’s main energy
source](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65644). The [U.S.
environmental
movement](https://michiganintheworld.history.lsa.umich.edu/environmentalism/exhibits/show/main_exhibit/origins)
continued to grow, and people got interested in natural gas as an alternative
to coal.

In response, coal companies doubled down on the fantasy of “clean” coal.

[![Two hands hold a lump of coal and a scrub brush and appear to be scrubbing
the lump of coal. It says 'Can coal be cleaned before it's burned? Yes. Inside
and
out!'](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733172/original/file-20260430-86-877q4j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/733172/original/file-20260430-86-877q4j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)An
American Electric Power ad in The Wall Street Journal in 1976 talked about
cleaning coal. Wall Street Journal archive.

A [1979
advertisement](https://www.reddit.com/r/PropagandaPosters/comments/1wuku7/can_coal_be_cleaned_before_its_burned_newspaper/#lightbox)
for American Electric Power, for example, flew in the face of [Clean Air
Act](https://www.epa.gov/laws-regulations/summary-clean-air-act) mandates that
coal corporations employ “scrubbing” technology to remove sulfur dioxide from
smoke – the ad depicted someone cleaning coal by hand.

**The myth continues**

Today, [coal generates only 16.2% of America’s
electricity](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=427&t=3), down from
generating more than half of the U.S. power supply in the 1990s. But the
country isn’t done with it. Even though coal production today is far below its
peak, as companies [try to shut down old uneconomic
plants](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/20/climate/trump-coal-plant-centralia-
washington.html), Trump has [promised to “reinvigorate” the coal
industry](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2025/04/reinvigorating-americas-beautiful-clean-coal-industry-and-
amending-executive-order-14241/).

In addition to [ordering some coal plants to continue
operating](https://stateline.org/2026/03/19/trump-is-forcing-coal-plants-to-
stay-open-it-could-cost-customers-billions/), the Trump administration has
pulled out old coal promotion tactics from the past, including [repeatedly
referring to coal](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2025/04/reinvigorating-americas-beautiful-clean-coal-industry-and-
amending-executive-order-14241/) as “clean and beautiful.” One image inserts
Coalie next to a coal-mining family that otherwise looks like an ad that could
have appeared a century ago.

[![A drawing of a family with a cartoon coal lump looking like a
toy.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732966/original/file-20260429-57-eit40o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732966/original/file-20260429-57-eit40o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)A
2026 promotion for the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
includes a cartoon family with ‘Coalie’ added to the picture, looking like a
child’s toy. [OSMRE](https://www.osmre.gov/news/stories/10-things-know-about-
how-osmre-supports-americas-energy-legacy-and-communities)

And, like its predecessors, this picture tries to present an innocent image of
a product that [harms human health and the
environment](https://www.catf.us/resource/cradle-to-grave-the-environmental-
impacts-from-coal/).

A [2018 study](http://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.18444) found that black lung
disease was [on the rise in
Appalachia](https://www.npr.org/2018/02/06/583456129/black-lung-study-biggest-
cluster-ever-of-fatal-coal-miners-disease), where [about 40% of America’s
coal](https://www.datawrapper.de/_/zl7DI/) is mined today. Living near a
fossil-fuel power plant [exposes residents to
pollutants](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf4915) that [contribute to
premature deaths](https://theconversation.com/pollution-from-coal-power-
plants-contributes-to-far-more-deaths-than-scientists-realized-study-
shows-218231), asthma and lung cancer, including tiny particulate matter known
at PM 2.5, sulfur dioxide and mercury. Even when it’s just sitting in piles
waiting to be used at a power plant, coal [can harm human
health](https://theconversation.com/even-when-its-sitting-in-storage-coal-
threatens-human-health-80865) as the wind blows across it and carries coal
dust into the air and people’s lungs.

The myth of coal as healthy and family friendly has been around for centuries
– but coal has never been clean, or cute.![The
Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/281742/count.gif?distributor=republish-
lightbox-basic)
